name: Brazen Yellow
lede: Brazen Yellow is a warm, brassy yellow that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary traces back to 1590, one of three names the dictionary records for nearly the same plate position.

sections.title: One plate, three names over three centuries
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* (1930) places Brazen Yellow on plate 11, position L6, and gives it the earliest recorded use of the three names tied to this plate position, 1590 [1]. The same plate position carried the name *Brass* by 1654 and *Rattan* by 1921, so the dictionary shows the same color being renamed across three centuries without explaining why any one name displaced another [1]. The ISCC-NBS 1955 lists do not carry Brazen Yellow separately, and the National Bureau of Standards circular cites only Maerz and Paul's entry [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[zedoary-wash]], [[popcorn]] and [[dusty-amber]], at 3.5, 3.5 and 3.8 ΔE [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a color match to this swatch in 818 of 23,781 paintings, 3.44 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 673, more common than 86 percent of the named colors we track [3]. Sir Henry Raeburn is its most devoted painter, carrying it in 4 of the 12 [[painter:henry-raeburn|Raeburn]] paintings in the archive, 4.4 times the rate expected from the museums his works come from [3].

The color's deepest historical cluster is the 1300s, 3.1 times the expected rate across 251 paintings from that century, and inside a painting it most often plays an accent (60 percent of its 673 within-painting matches) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1236, more than three centuries before the name's 1590 record, which shows only that a similar-looking hue existed in paint long before the word did, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [3]. India is the most over-represented country, at 2.2 times its expected share, with the Kalighat and Mughal schools both well above the archive's average [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [3].
